# A Practical Guide to the Country of Almost

The country of Almost is easiest to reach by mistake.

Take a train that leaves without announcing its destination, or turn off a familiar road because a shop sign reminds you of someone you almost met. At some point, the conductor may ask whether you are going as far as your ticket says. When you reply that you had meant to go somewhere else, he will look at you with professional sympathy and suggest a change.

This is how the country begins: not with a dramatic border, but with the quiet suspicion that you may have chosen the wrong life.

Almost is often mistaken for a kingdom of regret, a place furnished with abandoned careers, unloved houses, and the glaring railway platforms of choices not taken. That would be a miserable sort of tourism. The country’s inhabitants are generally kinder. They do not keep souvenirs of failure. They preserve possibilities.

There is a distinction. A regret says, *I should have gone.* An almost says, *there was another arrangement of that afternoon.* The first closes a door loudly. The second leaves it open, not because the people behind it are necessarily better, but because the door has not yet been tested.

The country has green hills, rivers the color of weak tea, and towns whose names become difficult to remember while you are saying them. Its borders are porous. Its railways run on schedules of uncertain enthusiasm. The sun is not always in the correct place.

Visitors should bring curiosity, a tolerance for unfinished sentences, and no more certainty than they can comfortably carry.

## Entry Formalities

The principal border is a wooden booth painted the blue of a dusk that has not quite arrived. The officer inside is called a Registrar of Tendencies. He will ask for your passport, your itinerary, and your purpose in visiting.

You are permitted to answer any of the three with a question.

When I applied, the Registrar asked what I hoped to find.

“An answer,” I said.

“To which question?”

“The one I left outside.”

He considered this, compared two invisible documents, and stamped my passport with a small silver door. It opened nowhere in particular.

Customs is strict. Confident plans must be declared and surrendered. Perfectly timed itineraries are confiscated. Anything sealed in glass, labeled *this is what happens next*, will be refused unless you can explain why it is less alive than a pencil stub or a bus ticket used for a purpose you have forgotten.

I asked whether regret was taxed.

“Only the theatrical kind,” said the customs officer. “The genuine article is too heavy to lift.”

This is reassuring. In Almost, the disappointed do not pose at scenic overlooks. They are not rewarded for brooding. Nor are they expected to keep an endless ledger of roads not traveled. The country is interested in possibility, not in self-pity, and it reserves several fine prisons for people who insist that an unlived life was better than the one actually being lived.

The Registrar asked if I intended to stay long.

“I don’t know.”

“Excellent,” he said. “That is the beginning of a flexible visa.”

## Maps

Maps of Almost cannot be printed by ordinary machines. The paper is made from compressed hesitation, and the ink behaves strangely under strong light.

Roads to actual towns are drawn in firm black lines. Roads to probable towns appear as dotted lines. Roads to possibilities that depend upon your mood may be indicated by faint blue threads, usually found near the edges of the page.

I once unfolded a map of the northern provinces and discovered that my house stood on it. Not the house in which I was staying, but the one I might have bought with a better decision, six streets farther from the railway.

The location was marked **available**, although of course it was no longer available. I traced the route to it with one finger. The line wandered through a park that existed on rainy days and disappeared whenever the sun came out.

Cartographers here maintain two versions of every landscape. One shows what is there. The other shows what is nearly there: a bridge under construction, a theater awaiting its audience, a harbor with one imaginary ship preparing to leave.

A guide once explained the difference between a map and a memory.

“A map says, ‘This is the way you went.’ A memory says, ‘This is the way you believe you went.’ Almost is the country where the belief is allowed to remain visible.”

At first, the maps are daunting. Eventually, they become liberating. A blank space no longer seems like ignorance. It is simply a place for a different question.

## The Weather

The weather in Almost is determined less by the season than by the local consensus.

Tourist pamphlets describe the mornings as remembered, the afternoons as provisional, and the evenings as generally reliable but emotionally exaggerated. Rain often takes the form of something someone meant to say. Fog has the taste of a previous goodbye. On certain Tuesdays, the sun shines on everybody, though nobody can agree afterward whether it really did.

Forecasts are printed without temperatures:

**Partly certain of clouds.**  
**Likely rain, followed by sudden nostalgia.**  
**Clear with a moderate chance of alternate arrangements.**

The wind usually comes from elsewhere, which locals find embarrassing. If you ask where, they will say, “The place where the other decision was made.”

There is a particular quality to the air in the capital. It is not melancholy exactly, but it carries a faint suggestion of missed appointments. Children are advised not to linger there after dark, although nobody can say why. By morning, their shoes are often wet and their stories contain tunnels.

I have seen rain arrive as a conversation I had decided not to have. It rattled against the window for half an hour, then stopped just before the point at which I might have said the necessary thing.

That may have been luck. In Almost, even the weather respects suspense.

## The Capital: Likely

Likely is the capital of Almost, though its name is not officially attached to it. A municipal clerk explains that naming a place “Definitely” would produce too much administrative difficulty. The city is large enough without absolute certainty.

Its main avenue, the Boulevard of the Better Decision, leads from the station to a central square. At one end stands the railway; at the other, a statue of the founder.

The founder did not found the city. He came close, but was delayed by a series of small obligations. Nevertheless, the statue is impressive. The inscription reads:

**HERE STANDS A MAN WHO VERY NEARLY BEGAN SOMETHING.**

The square contains several such monuments. There is a bronze figure of the woman who almost wrote the national anthem, a fountain commemorating the inventor of a machine for recovering lost time, and a bench dedicated to the dog that might have been unusually intelligent.

The city is full of scaffolding. Not construction scaffolding—temporal scaffolding. Walkways extend into the future, stop at a narrow ledge, and stop again some yards later. Notices promise that completion is “pending understanding.”

The national parliament is called the Chamber of Consequential Differences. Its members debate matters such as whether the city should have been built beside the river, whether the southern road should have curved north, and whether the government ought to have resigned in a more decisive manner.

Debates are long. The important speeches are never delivered because everyone recognizes the moment at which the speech would have made a difference, and that moment is carefully avoided.

## The Museum of Unfinished Things

The Museum of Unfinished Things occupies a former customs warehouse. Its collections are arranged not by date, material, or artist, but by degree of incompleteness.

On the first floor are the small incompletions: a sentence interrupted by laughter, a bridge with one end waiting for the other, a dance begun before the music had settled on a key. A piano stands in the corner with a sheet of music entitled **Concerto for a pianist who almost learned to play.**

The second floor contains larger interruptions. There is a house with all the rooms except the one that would have been the owner’s. There is a painting in which the central figure remains unpainted, not because the artist lacked skill but because the person had not yet been invented.

The museum guide explains that every object has been preserved from at least one possible future.

“Not all of them actually happened,” she says. “That is rather the point. If everything happened, the collection would be a museum of facts. This is a museum of invitations.”

Visitors sometimes object. They ask whether the museum is full of things that do not exist. The guide replies that the objects are perfectly existent. It is their relationships that remain hypothetical.

A letter sits beneath glass. It begins:

*Dear—*

The paper is stained, as if it had been carried for years. The handwriting becomes firmer after the dash, then stops.

Beside it is a receipt for a train ticket purchased in a town that no longer exists, for a journey that may not have taken place. The receipt is genuine. The traveler’s name has been erased by rain.

In the final room, a plaque reads:

**THE LIFE YOU ARE LIVING: CURRENTLY UNAVAILABLE FOR EXHIBITION.**

I spent a long time there.

The museum does not tell you what you should have done. It asks only whether you can remain in the room a while without demanding an explanation.

The founding date of Almost is impossible to establish, which locals consider a charming distinction rather than a national embarrassment.

The first border was reportedly created when a traveler stood at a railway crossing and wished she had stayed. The wish lasted three days. During that period, the surrounding landscape became available to people whose plans had not quite worked out.

For many centuries, Almost had no government. Decisions were made by whoever happened to be standing nearer the matter. This produced impressive buildings and a number of administrative errors, but also excellent music.

The republic was formally established after a long debate about whether it needed establishing at all.

Its first leader was elected on a platform of promising nothing definite. He served two possible terms, one in fact and one in recollection. The second term is commemorated in statues, although several statues are now being reconsidered.

Almost has fought no wars, though it has nearly fought several. In one famous case, peace was declared forty minutes before the final treaty was signed. In another, an army marched to the border, discovered that the enemy had changed its mind, and went home embarrassed.

There is a meadow outside the capital with a small plaque:

**THE WAR THAT WAS NOT HERE.**

A fence surrounds it.

Most citizens regard the fence as excessive. A few argue that it is the only thing in the landscape with sufficient commitment. Beyond it lie wildflowers, insects, and a distant line of hills that may be moving.

The people of Almost are not waiting for you to discover your hidden talent. They will be pleased if you discover their company, but they are not in the business of rescue.

You may meet a baker who nearly became a sailor. She will show you the flour on her forearms and explain that the sea was not wrong; she simply had not been brave enough to board. She will not ask whether you think she should have gone.

You may meet a man who has spent forty years preparing to emigrate. He knows the climate of three countries, the names of four boats, and the precise location of the window he would have chosen. He will speak about all of this with great affection and no apparent intention of leaving.

The stranger tells you about a life you almost had. There is a blue kitchen. There is a dog with a particular bark. There are arguments about money and long walks after rain. You recognize none of it, and yet the details are strangely persuasive.

The stranger thanks you for listening.

Then you are asked what you would have done.

This is the dangerous part. The country is generous, but not without boundaries. It does not permit visitors to improve imaginary people.

A person’s possible self is not a saint because she stayed home. It is not a failure because she stayed. It has no claim upon your admiration. The most important fact about a possible life is that it has not happened.

The people of Almost are particularly skilled at telling jokes. Their humor is dry, local, and frequently incomprehensible to visitors who have not yet learned the trick of treating the future as a suggestion.

“Until I know what I came for.”

“Very good. We have a room.”

In the drawers are a pair of shoes that almost fit, a map with the destination omitted, and a note left by a previous guest:

*If you are reading this, you have almost woken up.*

Others add:  
*There is not.*

“I may not need it,” she said.

The price fell to half a perhaps.

The price fell again.

A country of Almost cannot be entered with a fixed itinerary. Its banks do not offer loans against future success. They will, however, lend you money against a future version of yourself, provided you can describe that version without becoming too attached.

“Compound the interest,” she says, without looking up.

Time in Almost is not measured by clocks. The clocks are present, but they disagree in a friendly manner.

A visitor can spend a week in Almost and return home believing only two days have passed. This is not always considered fraud. The country prefers to think of it as temporal generosity.

The people of Almost do not worship youth or resent age. They are more interested in sequence than in ranking. A thing that happened after another thing is later, even if the later thing is not better.

This makes their cemeteries unusual. The gravestones do not say how long a person lived. They say what came next.

*After the winter, she planted beans.*

*After the argument, he waited.*

*After the train, a different road.*

The inscriptions are factual. They do not say that the beans flourished, that the waiting ended well, or that the other road led anywhere worth mentioning.

## Departures

Departure is the most difficult part of visiting Almost. Entry requires a mistake, but leaving requires a decision.

The station is a small building near the river. Its departure board reads:

**Platform 1: Certain.**  
**Platform 2: Probable.**  
**Platform 3: If you are quite sure.**

I arrived at the station carrying a suitcase containing two shirts, a cracked notebook, and a map of the capital. In the notebook I had written down several things I had almost become, a list of people I had nearly spoken to, and one recipe for soup I had intended to make on a Sunday.

At the platform, a porter asked whether I was returning to my life.

“Yes,” I said.

“Your old one?”

I had not expected the question.

“No,” I said. “The current arrangement.”

He nodded as though this were a more sophisticated answer. The train was waiting beneath a roof that had almost collapsed. A sign above the carriage said:

**THIS TRAIN LEAVES AT 12:40, PROVIDED YOU HAVE DECIDED TO GO.**

I put my suitcase down and looked back toward the city. From there, Likely appeared almost ordinary. A bell sounded somewhere behind the rooftops. A person I might have met crossed the square, or perhaps only crossed the version of the square I had been imagining.

I thought about all the lives waiting in Almost: the brilliant, the ridiculous, the tender, the cruel, the ridiculously tender. I thought about how easy it was to call a life unlived when no one had to live it. No one had to be disappointed by the career, frightened by the freedom, or bored by the third week of the perfect house.

The porter cleared his throat.

“Does the train depart at 12:40?”

“I suppose so,” I said.

“That is not a time,” he replied. “It is a possibility.”

At that moment, the train left—three minutes early, according to the station clock, and seven minutes late, according to mine.

I boarded. The country of Almost slipped away behind the window, becoming less distinct with every mile. Its green hills looked almost like the hills of home. Its towns looked almost like the towns we had passed through before. Even the river, for a brief moment, seemed familiar in the way a word can seem familiar when heard in a dream.

I did not return with a new purpose, a recovered talent, or a message from my better self. I had not found a version of myself who spoke several languages, loved without fear, and knew when to leave.

I had found something less dramatic and more useful: the ability to remain briefly in the company of what might have been without insisting that it should have been.

That is not wisdom, exactly. It is only a kind of courtesy.

At the next station, I bought a ticket with a definite destination. The conductor punched a small hole in it. On the ticket, beneath the departure time, someone had printed:

**You are here, and you are going.**

I liked the sentence. It seemed to leave enough room for both.
